title: ABO & Rh Blood Grouping — Forward & Reverse Typing

references.label: AABB Technical Manual
references.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies (AABB)

references.label: CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

purpose: To determine a patient's or donor's ABO and Rh(D) blood type using both forward grouping (testing red cells against known antisera) and reverse grouping (testing serum/plasma against known reagent red cells), which must agree before a type is finalized.
principle: Forward grouping directly tests which antigens are on the person's red cells using anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D reagent antisera; reverse grouping independently tests the person's own serum/plasma against reagent A1 and B red cells to detect the expected reciprocal antibodies. Because a healthy person's ABO antigen and antibody status are reciprocal by definition (see the related principle concept), forward and reverse results should match — this built-in cross-check is why ABO typing is performed both ways rather than by forward typing alone.
requiredMaterials: Test tubes or typing card/gel system per the method in use
requiredReagents: Reagent A1 and B red cells (for reverse grouping)

procedure.instruction: Forward grouping: combine a red cell suspension from the patient/donor separately with anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D reagent antisera.
Centrifuge briefly (or follow the gel/card method's specified process) and examine each reaction for agglutination.
Reverse grouping: combine the patient's/donor's serum or plasma separately with reagent A1 cells and reagent B cells.
Centrifuge briefly and examine each reaction for agglutination.

procedure.note: A forward/reverse discrepancy is not simply reported — it triggers further investigation (e.g. weak subgroup, unexpected antibody, technical error) before any type is released for clinical use.
procedure.instruction: Compare forward and reverse results — they must be concordant with the expected reciprocal pattern for the ABO group; resolve any discrepancy per the laboratory's discrepancy-investigation procedure before finalizing a type.
Record the Rh(D) result from forward grouping; a negative or weak/discrepant D reaction may require a supplementary test per the laboratory's method before finalizing Rh status.

observations: Grade agglutination reaction strength in each tube/well/gel column and record concordance between forward and reverse results.
interpretation: A finalized ABO/Rh type requires forward-reverse concordance; discordant results must be resolved (never averaged or assumed) before the type is used for transfusion decisions.
precautions: Positive identification of the patient/donor and specimen is critical — a mislabeled specimen in blood banking carries severe patient-safety consequences.
Use only validated reagent antisera/cells within their expiration and storage requirements.
limitations: Weak or rare ABO subgroups can produce ambiguous forward/reverse results requiring specialized follow-up beyond routine typing.
This entry describes routine grouping; it is not a treatment or transfusion-decision algorithm.
biosafetyNotes: All blood specimens and reagent red cells are biohazardous; follow standard precautions and the laboratory's blood bank-specific chain-of-custody/labeling procedures.
